source_message.speaker: client
source_message.text:
Hey Larry — I went through the BOM and overall I really like the direction. This is exactly what I was hoping for.

A few thoughts I’d like your input on before we move forward:

• Motors — I’m wondering if 200 RPM might be a bit low for achieving a strong, frothy matcha texture. Do you think it makes sense to increase RPM while still maintaining enough torque for smooth mixing?

• Whisk — would a stainless steel or milk-frother-style head perform better than the resin whisk in terms of consistency, durability, and foam quality?

• Spout — I’d like to stick with the solenoid approach. It’s important that the pour is clean, controlled, and seamless (mix → open → pour) both for texture and the overall visual experience.

• Splash / mess control — this is really important for events. I want to make sure:
– minimal to no splashing during mixing
– smooth, controlled flow from the spout (no sputtering)
– no dripping when the valve is closed
– good sealing so nothing leaks into the base
– some form of splash guard or lip around the bowl if needed

• Cleaning — I’d like the bowls and spout components to be easy to clean or removable if possible.

Everything else looks great to me. Curious to hear your thoughts on these and if you’d adjust anything before we finalize the BOM.

value_updates.cleaning_access: Bowl removal should support easy cleaning between uses.

source_message.speaker: freelancer
source_message.text:
For the motors, I believe you are right about the speed. I've selected some new ones that will spin at 1000RPM. The PWM controller will still allow the speed to be adjusted from 0 up to 1000 while still maintaining the torque to mix the liquids. 

The whisk portion is tricky, there aren't a lot of options with the requirements we need. You want a decently sized mixing head to ensure the bowl is mixed well. The bowl is approximately 9 inch in diameter while the plastic mixing head on the BOM is only around 2.4" diameter. The original wire whisk I suggested was around 4.5" in diameter. Despite it being listed for a 6qt bowl, I do think it has the potential to work well in our smaller bowl. I think the ideal mixing head would be similar to the handheld electric frothers/mixers but those heads only come in very small sizes. 

I don't foresee splashing to be an issue. The motors can be adjusted on the fly if the mixing becomes too rough. If splashing is an issue a simple splash guard can be installed as you suggested.

For cleaning, as of now the bowl is designed to be removed very simply. I also plan to allow for the custom spout to be removable for easy cleaning as well. 

Overall I think we are nearly ready, I'll change the motor to 1000rpm. For the whisk, perhaps we should pick 2 styles to test which works best? The whisk is probably one of the easiest components to swap to new design if needed. A simple adapter should let us attach basically any whisk to our setup.

execution.observed_behavior: Freelancer reports that the current bowl design provides very simple removal for cleaning.

source_message.speaker: client
source_message.text:
A couple things I want to make sure we dial in as you refine the layout:

• Bowl removal — I want to make sure the bowls can be lifted out easily without interference from the whisk or motor assembly.

• Whisk removal — ideally something quick and simple to detach (no tools if possible), since cleaning and swapping during events will be important.

• Whisk positioning — I think getting the height right will be key for both foam quality and minimizing splashing, especially with the higher RPM range.

• Splash control — since we’re going with a stronger motor, I want to make sure the system stays clean during operation (either through positioning, bowl geometry, or a subtle guard if needed).

Everything is looking great — just want to make sure we get these usability details right for real event use.

value_updates.removal_clearance: Bowls must lift out easily without interference from the whisk or motor assembly.

source_message.speaker: freelancer
source_message.text:
I'll check clearance height for the spouts today but it should be just a little over 5 inches. Maybe around 5.5. drain path from bowls to spouts will be completely hidden. Once a bowl is removed it is visible somewhat until a new bowl is placed in.
The whole system will be easily serviceable. The top and bottom panels are able to be removed if ever needed to service the machine. The towers for the motors are also able to be opened if needed to service the motors themselves.
Bowls will be easy to remove still.

execution.observed_behavior: Freelancer reports that the integrated tower spacing and motor placement still allow the bowls to be removed easily.

source_message.speaker: client
source_message.text:
Hey Larry, The latest updates are looking great. Seeing the plumbing, drainage routing, bowl integration, and overall structure come together has me even more excited about where this is heading. As I’ve been thinking ahead, one thing that keeps coming to mind is the possibility of eventually using the Matcha Mixer in a retail location if we move forward with opening a shop. Because of that, I wanted to start thinking about food-service and health department considerations early while we’re still in the prototype stage. A few things I’d love to keep in mind as the build progresses: 
 Food-contact materials (stainless steel, food-grade plastics, food-grade silicone, etc.) Ease of cleaning and sanitation Making sure there aren’t any hidden areas where liquid can collect or become trapped Easy removal of bowls, whisks, and components for cleaning Separation between liquids and electrical components Accessibility for maintenance and servicing if something ever needs to be replaced When you get a chance, I’d also love to know what materials are being used in the food-contact areas and whether there are any areas you see as potential sanitation or cleaning challenges. Long term, I think it would be helpful to keep documentation on: 
 materials used CAD files wiring layout cleaning procedures exploded-view drawings if available Not because we need all of that right now, but because if this evolves into something bigger, having that information could be incredibly valuable. Overall, everything is looking fantastic and I’m really excited to see the testing videos and final assembly. It’s amazing seeing the project move from an idea into a real machine. 

Karla Burton
